Utility-based variable selection to improve clinical utility of prediction models: the NBvarsel R package

Lasai Barreñada<sup>1,2</sup>, Andrew Vickers<sup>3</sup>, Laure Wynants<sup>1,2,4</sup>, Dirk Timmerman<sup>1,5</sup>, Ewout Steyerberg<sup>6</sup>, Ben Van Calster<sup>1,2,6</sup>

**Abstract: 250 words max**

**Objective:** Variable selection (VS) for clinical prediction models is mostly done purely based on statistical grounds, either using information criteria or p-values. These approaches ignore the cost of misclassifications and the cost of measuring a variable. We propose a decision analytic VS based on net benefit and implement it in the open-source _NBvarsel_ R package.

**Materials and Methods:** The proposed algorithm selects the set of predictors by exhaustively comparing the net benefit of all combinations using cross validation, with an extension based on backward elimination for large dimensional settings. It provides variable importance as the contribution of each predictor to the utility and allows the user to set cost of measuring a predictor. We illustrate the usage of the package in a simulation and test the performance in terms of discrimination, calibration clinical utility in three real case studies.

**Results:** Across the three case studies, _NBvarsel_ obtained a more parsimonious model maintaining or improving the clinical utility with minimal loss of discrimination and calibration. If costs of selecting a predictor are considered the method rules out costly predictors that contribute little to utility.

**Discussion:** _NBvarsel_ serves as a promising approach for integrating clinical utility directly into the variable selection process allowing prediction models to maximize patient benefit while minimizing unnecessary clinical burden.

**Conclusion:** We present an easy-to-use algorithm based on the utility that a model would have in the clinic to select the best subset of predictors, which leads to simpler models maintaining the same utility.

# Introduction

Determining a patient's condition based on their current characteristics is called diagnosis and is key to initiate any treatment and minimize future complications. Different conditions require exploring different characteristics. For example, a bone fracture can be diagnosed through medical imaging and COVID-19 through a PCR test. Clinical prediction models are statistical tools that estimate the probability that a patient has or will develop a condition in the future \[1\]. These models try to link the outcome (event or condition) with a series of predictors in a dataset, a task often called supervised learning \[2\]. These predictors should be information readily available at the time of diagnosis, not too costly to measure and measured with reasonable precision \[1\]. However, there might be a vast number of predictors that meet these criteria and selecting among them is needed \[3\].

Variable selection, best subset selection, feature selection, and feature engineering are terms used in prediction modelling to describe the process of selecting which predictors to use when training a model. Different approaches for variable selection have been presented. Heinze and colleagues \[4\] categorized them into five groups based on the criteria to select the variables: (1) based on significance testing, (2) based on information criteria (e.g. AIC, BIC), (3) based on penalized likelihood (e.g. LASSO, elastic-net), (4) based on change-in-estimate or performance (e.g. backward elimination, stepwise selection), or (5) based on background or domain knowledge. Across machine learning literature, it is often observed that variable selection methods are grouped into filter, wrapper and embedded methods \[5\]. Filter methods use statistical properties to select variables and are therefore equivalent to significance testing and information criteria-based approaches. Wrapper methods, in contrast, use model performance to select the best subset, which corresponds to Heinze's change-in-estimate criterion. Finally, embedded methods perform variable selection as part of the model training; this includes penalized likelihood but also other approaches such as feature importance calculation in tree-based or genetic algorithms \[6,7\]. This work will focus on change-in-estimate or wrapper methods for variable selection in clinical prediction models.

To be used in clinical practice, prediction models need to show good performance in external validation in terms of discrimination (area under the ROC curve), calibration (calibration plot), and clinical utility (Net Benefit, NB) \[8\]. Variable selection is usually performed by considering only the statistical properties of the predictors (filter methods), without accounting for the clinical benefit or utility. Utility refers to the quality of decision-making when a risk model is used to decide whether a patient requires treatment \[9\]. Models that are not clinically useful are more likely to be forgotten quickly or even never be implemented in real practice \[10\]. Consequently, we aim to include clinical utility in the model development process through a clinical utility guided variable selection.

Utility values, relating to misclassification costs (i.e., the benefit of treating the diseased and the harm of treating the healthy), are hard to elicit at an absolute scale. However, it is known that the ratio of harm to benefit is directly related to the decision threshold for classifying a patient as high risk \[9\]. NB, a simple metric for clinical utility, uses this relationship. NB is calculated as benefit minus harm multiplied by scaled by the harm-to-benefit ratio \[11\]. In statistical terms, this is the number of true positives minus the number of false positives weighted by the harm-to-benefit ratio. This ratio reflects how many false positives a clinician is willing to accept per true positive. For example, if a surgeon is willing to perform 9 surgeries on benign tumors to catch 1 malignant tumor, the exchange rate is 1/9, corresponding to a 10% decision threshold. However, NB should often be presented across a range of thresholds, given variability across clinicians and settings \[12\]. The use of NB and related metrics to evaluate a new variable was discussed by Baker and colleagues \[13\] but it has never been implemented as a variable selection algorithm for clinical prediction models.

The aim of this paper is therefore to develop a simple and interpretable variable selection algorithm based on clinical utility to determine which predictors to include in the model and implement it as an easy to use R package. Additionally, we will explore the effect on performance of the method. We will use and implement the method in the context of a logistic regression to estimate the probability of a binary outcome, but the rationale extends to more flexible machine learning or AI probabilistic algorithms.

# Methodology

## Algorithm

The problem we aim to address is defined as follows: given a set of predictors and a modelling algorithm we seek the subset of that maximises the net benefit:

Here, denotes the (adjusted) net benefit of algorithm with predictors for the decision threshold . The parameter may be a single value, or a range of clinically relevant values specified based on clinical context. In cases where a range of values is used, we want to maximize the average NB across that range.

The proposed variable selection algorithm does not involve modifying coefficient estimation, since the logloss minimisation (or log-likelihood maximisation) is known to provide coefficients with good properties \[14\]. Therefore, the proposed algorithm works as follows:

- Define all possible model combinations based on the predictors:
- Assign a test tradeoff or (see section 2.3) to each predictor or group of predictors to adjust the NB accordingly. If the harm is unknown, this can be 0 and unadjusted NB will be used.
- Train models and evaluate their net benefit using cross validation with folds (default is 5).
  - This step can be parallelized to reduce computation time.
  - Nonlinearities can be addressed with restricted cubic splines.
  - Interactions can be included; we limit this option to either all pairwise interactions or no interactions.
- Rank the models based on NB and select the model with optimal NB.

Code implementing the NB based variable selection and the associated visualizations are available in the open-source R package _NBvarsel_ **(**[**https://lasaibarrenada.github.io/NB_varsel/**](https://lasaibarrenada.github.io/NB_varsel/)**, Box 1)**

### Large dimensional settings

The algorithm presented in section 2.1 becomes computationally too demanding when the number of candidate predictors increases. For a dataset with 20 candidate predictors, there are more than one million predictor combinations; consequently, the method fits 5 million models when using 5-fold cross-validation. In most trials or observational studies, the sample size is limited; therefore, the number of candidate predictors should also be kept small. Our methodology should always be used in compliance with these sample size criteria as explained in section 2.2. However, in those cases where the dimensionality of the data is large (e.g. electronic health records), we propose an extension of the methodology that we called groupwise (as opposed to exhaustive) NB variable selection.

In this extension, instead of calculating all the possible combinations, we use backward elimination with a number of predictors per step specified ( yielding a total of model combinations per step. The fastest version ( therefore would fit models by removing a single predictor in the first iteration. Then the model with best performance is selected, if that model is the model where all predictors are used, that is selected as the best model, else the predictor(s) that were removed in the model with best performance are removed and the process is iteratively repeated until reaching the optimal model. Allowing values of higher than one is highly recommended if there is intuition of important interaction effects between predictors.

## Note on Sample size

Across systematic reviews of prediction model development and validation studies, a common issue is that there is no rationale for the sample size used \[15,16\]. International guidelines for prediction modelling, such as TRIPOD+AI and PROBAST+AI, recommend always justifying sample size \[17,18\].

The ratio of the number of events and potential number of predictors is called events per variable (EPV) or events per potential predictor (EPP). We prefer the latter because it explicitly states that its value should always be based on **potential** predictors, prior to data-driven variable selection; otherwise, the coefficients will be biased \[19\]. In traditional logistic and linear regression, EPP indicates relationship between the number of coefficients to be estimated and the amount of available information. The first recommendations indicated that an EPP of greater than ten was adequate \[20,21\]. Some years later, several authors disputed this rule, concluding that there is no single EPP rule that would guarantee accurate estimation \[22-24\].

Moving beyond rules of thumb, Riley and colleagues have developed several minimum sample size calculation techniques for developing and validating multivariable binary, continuous and time-to-event models \[25-30\]. Recently, the group has published a general framework that applies both to linear models and to more flexible AI-based algorithms such as random forests \[31\], that had shown to be more "data hungry" \[32,33\]. These criteria are based on overfitting and optimism control and precise estimation of the intercept.

When sample data is limited, a two-stage approach is often recommended: first selecting a subset of predictors based on subject matter knowledge and then performing a data-driven variable selection \[1,34\]. **Because it is prone to overfitting like any data-driven process, the methodology presented here must always adhere to the recommended minimum sample size.**

## Test harms

The concept of placing benefit and harm on the same scale is the principle of NB and decision curve analysis (DCA), yet it has not been applied directly to variable selection. In this work, we aim to introduce this concept in model development by defining a **harm adjusted NB.** Harm is therefore accounted for twice. First, to calculate NB, we set a threshold that should be related to the test harm (**harm of misclassifying a patient**). Second, the **harm of measuring a predictor** is introduced in the NB scale by quantifying the minimal expected benefit required to measure a variable (**Box 2**). The harm of misclassifying a patient is widely discussed in the literature \[11,12\]. The harm of measuring a predictor can be quantified as the number of tests that a doctor is willing to perform to find an event, also known as test tradeoff (TT) \[9\]. If the number is higher, then the cost of the predictor is lower. However, specifying this number upfront might be difficult, therefore, the difference in NB () can be used to derive the). TT is defined as:

where is the NB difference between the model with the additional predictor and the model without the predictor. Imagine we have a model that predicts risk of ovarian cancer with age and ultrasound measurements of the lesion that has a NB of 0.2. We wonder whether measuring CA125, that requires a blood sample, and including it in the model is cost-effective from the CgNB perspective. Given the monetary costs and test burden, practitioners suggests that they would be willing to measure CA125 in 100 patients to find an event. This means that we would be willing to include the predictor only if the NB increases by at least 0.01 (). By doing so, the researcher can specify the harm in terms of how many tests per true positive are needed to justify the inclusion of that predictor. For some predictors, such as age or sex, the harm is minimal, hence the TT can be high, meaning that almost any improvement justifies their inclusion. However, other predictors might have a higher associated harm such as a CT-scan which involves monetary costs, discomfort, exposure to radiation, etc... Harmful predictors have low TT, therefore the expected increase in utility must be higher. Quantifying these harms might be difficult and will have an important impact on the models. Some predictors might have shared harms; for instance, a single blood sample could extract information on several predictors. In those cases, the harm of only one or all of those predictors is identical, and the adjusted NB is calculated accordingly. If harms are omitted, the model would select variables based solely on standard NB.

## Variable importance

When the TT or is difficult to quantify, an alternative approach to help decide which variable to include in a model is computing each variable's contribution to the clinical utility. Variable importance is typically assessed using the statistical properties of the model being analysed. For instance, in a logistic regression model, coefficients can be used to compare the relative contribution of each predictor, while in random forest the Gini importance is often used to rank predictors by their contribution to the reduction of impurity. Other model-agnostic procedures have been proposed in the explainable AI field \[35\], such as the SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values and Local interpretable model-agnostic explanations (LIME) \[36,37\]. However, these techniques assess variable importance based on predicted probabilities rather than the clinical utility of the model. In his seminal paper introducing random forests, Breiman introduced permutation variable importance \[38\]. The algorithm proceeds as follows:

- A model is trained on training data.
- The performance of the model is evaluated on test or unobserved data.
- The performance of the model on test data is recalculated by randomly shuffling (permuting) values of a predictor .
- The variable importance of P is the difference between the performance on the true dataset and on the permuted dataset.

We apply this approach to calculate the average contribution of each predictor to the NB across the different predictor combinations evaluated. The permuted performance is calculated within the same folds of the cross-validation to ensure that the permuted and original performances are comparable. It is important to note that this variable importance is the average across all evaluated predictor combinations; therefore, the results might be distorted due to unrealistic combinations.

This simple illustration serves as an example on how the best subset of predictors based on performance in statistical terms does not necessarily mean better cost-utility. Then, using the same data generating mechanism we generated a larger test dataset (N = 100,000) for the three possible models. **Table S1** presents the results of the three models in 1000 bootstrap samples. In **Figure S1** we illustrate the harm adjusted decision curves (A) of the three models and flexible calibration curves (B). The best model according to the harm-adjusted NB is always the NBvarsel model. The right plot illustrates that calibration for that model is slightly worse, showcasing the need to find a balance between statistical performance and decision-making.

# Case studies

We will test the variable selection methodology (NBvarsel) with three datasets previously used to develop clinical prediction models. We will then compare the performance in terms of discrimination (AUC), calibration (calibration plots and OE ratio) and clinical utility (NB and DCA). All the analyses were performed using R version 4.4. We share complete R code to replicate all the results presented in this paper in the OSF repository (Link), although for the ovarian cancer and non-typhoidal salmonella, data is not publicly available.

## Ovarian cancer diagnosis - IOTA data

The optimal management of patients with an ovarian tumour depends on the histology of the mass. Benign masses do not always need to be removed and can be monitored with ultrasound follow up \[39\]. According to a recent study with 2 year follow-up, most of these masses spontaneously resolve, which reduces the risk of surgical complications \[40\]. If the mass is malignant, management in specialised oncology centers is suggested \[41\]. The IOTA group has developed and implemented several prediction models that use ultrasound and clinical characteristics to estimate the risk of malignancy of ovarian masses preoperatively \[42\]. In 2014, the ADNEX model was published using data from the IOTA phases 1-3 (N = 5909 , events = 1929) \[43\]. The model has shown excellent performance across different settings and populations, as shown in recent systematic reviews and meta-analyses \[15,44\]. ADNEX is a multinomial model that predicts the risk of benign, borderline, stage I invasive cancer, stage II-IV invasive cancer or metastatic cancer. In this work, we will treat it as a binary model, where the risk of malignancy is equal to the sum of the four malignant subtypes. As a validation dataset we will use IOTA phase 5 study (N = 6847, events = 1713) which was prospectively collected to externally validate ADNEX \[45\].

The variable selection procedure is detailed in the supplementary material of the original publication \[43\], we refer the reader there for details. The original ADNEX model utilized nine predictors: three clinical (age, serum CA125, and center type) and six ultrasound-based (lesion diameter, solid tissue proportion, >10 cyst locules, number of papillary projections, acoustic shadows, and ascites). While family history was initially considered, it was excluded during the variable selection process. For our analysis, missing CA125 values were handled via a regression-based imputation using all other ADNEX predictors, following recent methodological recommendations \[46\]. Then this model was applied to the development and validation dataset to impute missing values. In the validation dataset, some of the tumours were classified as uncertain for various reasons. In the published validation study, these values were also imputed with multiple imputation. We use one set of those imputed values for our analysis.

We extended the original predictor set with five additional features: bilateral masses (Yes/No), irregular internal cyst walls (Yes/No), Doppler color score (4 levels), maximum solid component diameter, and lesion-associated pain (Yes/No). The distribution of predictors by outcome for the training and test dataset is included in **Table S2**. In total 65,536 predictor combinations were evaluated across decision thresholds from 1% to 20% risk with 20-fold cross validation. This means that the average NB across those thresholds is the metric to optimize. We then compute discrimination in terms of AUC, OE ratio, clustered calibration and DCA \[47\]. Adjusted NB was also calculated with harms based on three group of variables: clinical history variables (no cost, should be available for all patients from the records), ultrasound based variables (TT = 200), blood based variables (TT = 80). We compared NB based variables selections to LASSO and backward elimination.

### Results

All models removed family history of ovarian cancer. The LASSO model also removed presence of papillary projections. NBvarsel models removed instead maximum diameter of the solid part of the tumour and in addition the adjusted NBvarsel removed CA125 biomarker. According to the variable importance calculations, the least important predictor was family history, and the most important one was the proportion of solid tissue (**Figure S2**).

The models showed comparable performance, with BE and NBvarsel approaches outperforming slightly the rest **(Table 3)**. All models tended to underestimate the risk of malignancy as shown in the clustered calibration plots with the backward elimination method yielding slightly closer curve to the diagonal (**Figure S3**). Clinical utility of all models was comparable except for ADNEX with CA125 and Lasso that showed slightly lower utility, as shown in the decision curves **(Figure 3, left)**, but when the costs of measuring a predictor are accounted for, the NBvarsel adjusted and ADNEX without CA125 had higher NB across the whole range of decision thresholds due to removing the costly CA125 predictor **(Figure 3, right)**. All-subset plots are available in Supplementary material (**Figures S4-S5**)

## Emergency department hospitalization - MIMIC IV ED (Large dimensional setting)

For the second case study we will use the well-known MIMIC IV emergency department (MIMIC IV ED) data combined with the MIMIC IV to predict the risk of hospitalization after visiting the emergency department \[48-50\]. MIMIC IV ED contains electronic health records data collected retrospectively from more than 425,000 emergency department stays in the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, between 2011 and 2019. We use the benchmark proposed by Xie et al., but with the latest version of MIMIC IV (v3.1) and MIMIC ED (v2.2) \[51\]. The authors propose this benchmark to allow different model developers to make fair comparisons when using MIMIC IV data, therefore we followed the same procedure to obtain the training and test data according to their guidelines (see <https://github.com/nliulab/mimic4ed-benchmark/tree/main>). The training data contains 334,420 (80%) patients and the testing data 83,605 (20%).

They propose 64 predictors to develop models to predict risk of hospitalization when a patient arrives to the emergency department, and they develop models using different algorithms, but we will focus on the LR model, that we denote as baseline model. Hospitalization happens when the patient is admitted to an inpatient care site immediately after the visit to the emergency department. The prevalence of hospitalization was 47%. The predictor distribution across test and training datasets is identical and is displayed in **Table S3**. If we were to use the exhaustive approach as in the ovarian cancer case this would mean approximately (million trillion) combinations, which is obviously not feasible. Therefore we will use the groupwise approach designed for large dimensional settings with group sizes 1 and 2. We used the algorithm with 5 cross validations and variables where selected with average NB across the whole range of decision thresholds. The authors selected the optimal decision threshold as the point nearest to the upper-left corner of the ROC curves (0.446). It is not recommended to define decision threshold using data driven approaches \[52\]. We used the whole range because we expect the threshold to hospitalize a patient to be very flexible, depending on hospital resources and context.

### Results

The algorithm with group size = 1 trains 65 models, followed by 64 in the next step, and so on. For MIMIC IV-ED dataset, 8 predictors were removed using this algorithm and the process took 1.45 hours. The method with group size of two iteratively removes predictors in pairs, so it accounts for interactions of two predictors. This method is computationally more intensive because the algorithm needs to train 2017 models in first step, followed by 1953 and so on. In the data, the algorithm removed 12 predictors in 6 steps.

The most important predictors according to NBvarsel were triage acuity (Emergency Severity Index) and age of the patient (**Figure S6**). The most important variables for NBvarsel were similar to those reported in the original study calculated using RF \[51\]. Baseline model and groupwise approaches obtained similar AUC (0.81). Calibration was slightly closer to the diagonal for the groupwise variable selection but tended to overestimate high risk more than the baseline approach (**Figure S7**). NBvarsel models consistently ranked slightly higher for clinical utility across the decision curve except for very high thresholds were baseline was more useful (**Table 3, Figure 4**).

## Non typhoidal Salmonella (NTS) - DeNTS trial

The last case study will use prospective cohort data to predict the risk of non-typhoidal Salmonella (NTS) bloodstream infection in children under five to guide the choice of empirical antibiotics \[53\]. The dataset contains clinical information collected prospectively from 2,327 paediatric hospital admissions with severe febrile illness at the Kisantu district hospital in the Democratic Republic of Congo (**Table S4**). We use the a priori clinical predictors proposed by Tack et al., applying their exact variable definitions and restricted cubic spline transformations for continuous predictors. The authors propose this specific set of predictors based on a systematic literature review to ensure clinical relevance and avoid data-driven bias; therefore, we followed the same procedure to obtain our variables according to their guidelines. They propose 11 predictors to develop models for antibiotic triage, and they develop a simplified clinical scoring system alongside it, but we will focus on their main multivariable logistic regression (LR) model.

In their work, variables were selected using a double backward elimination process and the final model was fitted using Firth's correction \[54\]. We will compare their approach to the introduced NBvarsel including splines for continuous predictors and then fitting the final model also using Firth's correction. In our algorithm, continuous predictors were introduced either with splines or were removed. The authors propose the reasonable range of thresholds to be between 20% and 50% so this were the range of thresholds used in the variable selection procedure.

If we were to use the exhaustive variable selection approach as in previous case studies, this would mean evaluating exactly 2,047 combinations. No test data was available; therefore, we present apparent results first and then we corrected for optimism and compare the published approach and our algorithm across 1000 bootstrap samples. The bootstrap included the NB based variable selection and the published variable selection.

### Apparent performance

According to NBvarsel, the model removed age, nutritional status and haemoglobin levels and the most important predictors were malaria status, duration of fever and respiratory rate (**Figures S8-S9**). Individual risks varied considerably among the published model and the NBvarsel model(**Figure 5**). AUC was slightly higher for the published model (0.80 vs 0.79). The calibration of the model was closer to the diagonal for NBvarsel model for estimated risk below 45% but tended to estimate too low risks in higher estimated probabilities (Figure **S10**). The NBvarsel model had higher NB from decision thresholds of 25% till 55% (**Figure S11**).

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 5. Distribution of individual risks for the model based on NB variable selection and the published model stratified by outcome. Plots in the margin depict densities per outcome. NTS: Non-typhoidal salmonella.

### Bootstrap results

Age at admission and malnutrition status were selected more than 50% of the bootstraps by the published strategy and were only picked up by NBvarsel 9% and 33% of the times. For the rest of predictors all were either selected more or less than 50% of the time in both strategies (**Figure S12**)

Discrimination and calibration metrics showed similar results for both models (**Table 4**). However, the median NB across the reasonable range of decision thresholds was superior for NBvarsel across the range of reasonable thresholds (**Figure 6**).

# Discussion

## Summary of Key Findings

While classical statistical properties are widely used to build clinical prediction models, relying solely on them for variable selection often fails to optimise clinical benefit and to account for the real-world burden of measuring predictors. To address this gap, we developed and implemented a variable selection algorithm as an easy-to-use R package that determines the optimal subset of predictors by exhaustively exploring all predictor combinations and maximizing clinical utility, measured via harm-adjusted or traditional NB. Through our simple illustration and three case studies, we showed that this decision analysis-based approach effectively reduces model complexity, maintaining comparable discrimination, calibration and clinical utility. In the ovarian cancer case study, adjusting for measurement harm successfully removed the CA125 biomarker, a test requiring a blood draw, while maintaining comparable performance to traditional backward elimination and LASSO methods. Furthermore, we showed that by using a groupwise elimination approach, this methodology can be successfully scaled to high-dimensional datasets like MIMIC IV-ED, yielding slightly higher clinical utility across decision thresholds compared to baseline models, and reducing the final parameters in the model (**Table 5**).

## Interpretation of Results

The results highlight that the "best" model in purely statistical terms (e.g., maximizing AUC or using AIC/BIC) is not necessarily the most useful model in clinical practice. Purely statistical metrics do not have the ability to balance correctly identified cases and harms of misclassifying a patient as done through NB. In addition our approach accounts for harms of measuring predictors as a crucial layer for variable selection. For instance, in our simulated illustration, ignoring test harms led to the inclusion of predictors that offered negligible improvements in NB at a disproportionate measurement cost. By translating the clinical burden into a TT, the minimum number of tests a doctor is willing to perform per true positive to justify the cost, our algorithm penalizes "expensive" predictors (**Box 2**). Consequently, models developed using this algorithm are naturally more parsimonious and tailored for pragmatic clinical implementation, as seen in the DeNTS trial data where the NB-based model achieved a better median NB in the 25% to 55% threshold range while requiring fewer predictors.

## Contextualization Within Existing Literature

There is growing recognition in the field of clinical prediction modelling that traditional performance measures are insufficient to guarantee a model's clinical value (Steyerberg, 2019; Van Calster et al., 2025). However, embedding utility directly into the variable selection phase has historically been difficult. While Baker et al. (2012) discussed the use of NB to evaluate new markers, it was not operationalized as an automated variable selection algorithm. Preliminary efforts to add utility to variable selection have struggled with the generation of utility values and the complexity of the methods \[55\]. Fouskakis and colleagues proposed using stochastic optimization to select the model with the best cost-adjusted Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC). The cost-adjusted BIC extends standard model selection by penalizing the total measurement cost of predictors rather than solely the number of variables included. However, implementing this method requires the specification of a cost-penalized prior, a task that proves difficult for clinicians who must quantify the trade-off between statistical gain and data collection burden. Zhao and Yu, developed a cost-sensitive variable selection method based on the -norm \[56\]. Their work is mainly methodological, without linking it to underlying utility of predictors. The _glmnet_ package in R allows to use weights that can represent misclassification costs \[57\]. The misclassification costs are used to estimate the model coefficients, therefore providing miscalibrated models, similar to class imbalance corrections \[58\]. The package also allows to determine penalty factors (i.e. predictor costs). The predictor's cost in the package can only be determined in relative terms without clinical translation, and they do not provide a combined cost approach which is common in medical settings. Our approach bridges this methodological gap by using "simple" metrics such as NB and the TT that have a clear clinical meaning, providing a much more intuitive scale for clinicians to quantify the harm-to-benefit ratio.

## Limitations

Despite its advantages, this methodology has several limitations. First, determining the specific "harm" of measuring a predictor is subjective, highly context-dependent, and challenging to quantify precisely prior to model development (**Box 2**). There might be situations where the harm of measuring a predictor is established and we advise therefore to use the costs. However, for most situations where this is not possible, the algorithm can be safely used without costs and provide a variable importance metric based on NB. Second, this is a data-driven method and therefore it is prone to overfit if sample size is limited. We recommend using the algorithm at least with the minimum sample size recommended by Riley's method \[28\]. Third, the exhaustive evaluation of all predictor combinations is computationally intensive and becomes infeasible with many candidate predictors. This is a process that should be done only once for model development, and we provide and option to parallelize the process to reduce considerably the running time. Lastly, we only developed the variable selection methodology for logistic regression, but we aim to increase to other modelling algorithms as part of _NBvarsel_ package.

## Implications

Prediction models that require burdensome, invasive, or expensive data collection for only marginal statistical gains are rarely adopted in routine care \[10\]. By integrating clinical utility directly into the model training pipeline, developers can ensure that their final models are both statistically rigorous and practically viable. The open-source _NBvarsel_ (<https://lasaibarrenada.github.io/NB_varsel/>) R package and its associated visualizations provide researchers with accessible tools to make informed, utility-driven decisions about variable selection.

## Future Research

Future research should prioritize extensive, controlled evaluations of this methodology. Specifically, simulation studies are needed to determine the sample sizes required to prevent overfitting, compare the relative performance of exhaustive versus groupwise approaches, and assess the impact of threshold mismatches between training and testing phases. We also plan to expand the methodology's analytical capabilities. For the current binary logistic regression framework, future updates will introduce full control over variable interactions and spline terms. Furthermore, while we currently use the average NB across a reasonable threshold range, we aim to implement kernel smoothing to dynamically weight specific target thresholds. Another related approach to using clinical utility directly into parameter estimation would involve using harm-adjusted NB as the optimization criterion for a loss function in deep learning architectures \[59\]. Although the algorithm's fundamental rationale applies to any prediction model, the current software is limited to binary logistic regression; future iterations will support survival and time-to-event outcomes, alongside other modelling algorithms. Finally, this package is open-source and intended for continuous development, and we actively welcome contributions from the research community.

## Conclusion

Clinical utility should not be an afterthought reserved only for external validation. By integrating a harm-adjusted NB metric directly into the variable selection process, researchers can produce prediction models that maximize patient benefit while minimizing unnecessary clinical burden.
